title: Developments in Probabilistic Topology
text:
Below are some current studies that deal with (potentially adjacent) subjects in the intersection of topology and probability.


Bismut, Jean-Michel. 1984. “The Atiyah-Singer Theorems: A Probabilistic Approach. II. The Lefschetz Fixed Point Formulas.” Journal of Functional Analysis 57 (3): 329–48. https://doi.org/https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1236(84)90106-X.


Dunfield, Nathan M., and William P. Thurston. 2006. “Finite Covers of Random 3-Manifolds.” Inventiones Mathematicae 166: 457–521. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-006-0001-6.


Even-Zohar, Chaim. 2017. “Models of Random Knots.” Journal of Applied and Computational Topology 1: 263–96. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41468-017-0007-8.


Eynard, Bertrand. 2016. Counting Surfaces: CRM Aisenstadt Chair Lectures. 1st ed. Progress in Mathematical Physics. Birkhäuser Basel. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-7643-8797-6.


Morishita, Masanori. 2024. Knots and Primes: An Introduction to Arithmetic Topology. 2nd ed. Universitext. Springer Nature Singapore. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-99-9255-3.


Nicolaescu, Liviu I. 2014. “Complexity of Random Smooth Functions on Compact Manifolds.” Indiana University Mathematics Journal 63 (4): 1037–65. https://www.jstor.org/stable/24904252.


Parzanchevski, Ori, and Ron Rosenthal. 2016. “Simplicial Complexes: Spectrum, Homology and Random Walks.” Random Structures &Amp; Algorithms 50 (2): 225–61. https://doi.org/10.1002/rsa.20657.


Sawin, Will, and Melanie Matchett Wood. 2024. “Finite Quotients of 3-Manifold Groups.” Inventiones Mathematicae 237: 349–440. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-024-01262-4.

title: Richard A. Oh
text: Hi! My name is Richard, and I am a fourth-year undergraduate studying mathematics at Stanford University. I am interested in the intersection between topology and probability—in particular, how the notion of randomness might offer new perspectives on topology through probabilistic methods. Currently, I am curious about how the rich algebraic machinery associated with topology might serve as a bridge between these seemingly distant branches of mathematics.
